query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored sequential annealing treatment conducted in the post-solidification stage at temperatures in the range of 0.6–0.7 Tm will refine the lamellar interfaces in eutectic high-entropy alloys, thereby simultaneously increasing both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy produced by conventional casting, exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that serve as microcrack initiation sites under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Apply a sequential thermomechanical treatment consisting of post-solidification annealing at a temperature near 0.65 Tm for optimized time intervals, under controlled atmosphere conditions.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed immediately after solidification, within a temperature window of approximately 0.6–0.7 Tm, and under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation. The time intervals and cooling rates are optimized to refine the lamellar structure without causing coarsening or unwanted phase transformations.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined and more uniform lamellar interfaces with reduced internal boundary imperfections that lower stress concentrations, thus decreasing microcrack initiation.
generation.mechanism: Annealing near 0.65 Tm facilitates controlled atomic diffusion that repairs and sharpens the internal boundaries of the lamellar colonies. This refinement reduces defect sites that typically serve as initiation points for microcracks, enabling a better balance between dislocation motion and stress distribution. Consequently, both the strength and ductility are improved relative to the untreated state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline cast alloy, the tailored annealed alloy should exhibit statistically significant increases in both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility, alongside a lower density of microcrack initiation sites observed via microstructural analysis.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy processed by conventional casting without the post-solidification tailored annealing treatment.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only within the defined annealing temperature window (0.6–0.7 Tm) and may not occur if the temperature or annealing duration substantially deviates from the optimal range. In addition, alloys with significantly different compositions or initial microstructures might not respond similarly.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by established thermomechanical theories, the precise magnitude of strength and ductility improvements is uncertain and may depend on the exact annealing parameters and alloy composition, requiring experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one processed using the conventional casting method (baseline) and another subjected to the tailored sequential annealing treatment at ~0.65 Tm for optimized durations. Conduct a series of room-temperature tensile tests and detailed microstructural analyses (e.g., SEM and TEM) to compare lamellar interface quality and microcrack density.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis does not confirm a refined lamellar interface with reduced microcrack initiation, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

chosen.technique: tailored thermomechanical treatment with sequential annealing

chosen.why: This approach directly addresses the core performance limitation by decoupling the traditional trade-off between strength and ductility. By optimizing thermal treatment parameters, the intervention refines the microstructure to both enhance strength and activate additional ductile deformation mechanisms, thereby mitigating microcrack initiation at the internal boundaries of lamellar colonies. Its basis in standard thermomechanical processing techniques also makes it the most plausible intervention deliverable by a research group.
